source.title: Sensitivity and Generalization in Neural Networks: an Empirical Study
source.authors: Roman Novak; Yasaman Bahri; Daniel A. Abolafia; Jeffrey Pennington; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendix; no apparent truncation affecting the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains networks with true or random labels and measures generalization and sensitivity, reporting comparisons relevant to V1. It uses the random-label condition as part of a different empirical measure rather than reproducing the original study’s central fitting analysis.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 compares paired networks trained with true versus random labels and reports generalization gap, Jacobian norm, and transitions. The paper states that all networks in this comparison reached 100% training accuracy in both settings. The paper does not report training time for this comparison or results for shuffled pixels, Gaussian-noise inputs, varying corruption fractions, explicit regularization, or learning order.
record.test_reason: The matched true-label and random-label experiments directly demonstrate perfect training fit with unchanged architecture, hyperparameters and optimization procedure. Although sensitivity is the paper's main question, its reported training accuracy bears directly on V1. The comparison includes only pairs that achieved perfect fit, so it does not establish how often arbitrary configurations succeed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: random labels are associated with higher sensitivity and poorer generalization, and the input-output Jacobian norm predicts generalization across many tested settings. Transition counts are less reliable, especially across optimizers and network sizes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares trained networks under true and random labels and measures generalization gap and sensitivity; it does not present a direct reproduction of the original studies’ random-label fitting analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset is CIFAR10 for the paired random-label comparison; transition counts do not track generalization in all considered scenarios, failing for optimizer comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-label networks have higher input-output Jacobian norms than their matched true-label counterparts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitting random labels produces greater input sensitivity than fitting true labels in matched fully connected image classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: Transition counts track the sensitivity and generalization difference in the random-label comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-label fitting changes the linear-region structure near image data relative to true-label fitting.

record.problems: The random-label comparison is shown in plots without exact values in the supplied text. It reports 100% training accuracy, but does not state separate test error values or details of the random-label assignment procedure. Results concern fully-connected networks on CIFAR10; the paper says extension to more complex architectures is future work.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows left out. Figure 4 results are figure-only; no precise values can be recovered from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error is not established by readable numerical results. The random-label generation procedure is unspecified, and success rates across all attempted configurations are not reported.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and progressively worsening test performance across intermediate label-corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing explicit regularization.
The order in which shared real-data patterns and noisy labels are learned.

missing.what: Add a training-accuracy result: both members of the selected true/random-label CIFAR10 pairs achieved 100% accuracy on the whole training set, with architecture, hyperparameters and optimization procedure matched. State explicitly that pairs were selected for successful fitting; no denominator or failure rate is supplied.

record.verdict_notes: The training-accuracy evidence supports existence of perfect random-label fits, not universal trainability. Fixed training budgets do not establish equal convergence times. Randomizing labels tests memorization capacity rather than explicitly training a model to exhibit a separately specified behavior.

versions.untested_parts: The text compares true and random labels, but does not specify the random-label assignment procedure or provide separate test error values.

rows.check: Generalization gap equals test error for these perfectly fitted networks, so this measure bears on V1. Perfect training accuracy is an inclusion criterion recorded as a condition; it needs its own result row.
